docs.title: why this garden exists
docs.text: i honestly saw the idea of a digital garden and noticed i had a similar sort of thing going on with my journal system at the time. i switched to notion and then obsidian and finally landed here. my own custom site where i can be authentically myself, learn in public, and grow alongside my thoughts.

docs.title: what belongs here
docs.text: everything i have ever thought about twice. that is my general rule. if i thought about it more than once it is ingrained in my head and i should nurture it like i would a living plant.

docs.title: how notes grow
docs.text: notes are thoughts. thoughts are ever evolving. if i think it twice i plant it. if i come across new information i fertilize. if the thought no longer serves it's purpose where it is, it get's composted to help make room for other ideas. it's all a metaphor but it is also quite literally how i garden in real life.

docs.title: how I learn and create
docs.text: i really just let my everything flow free. if i have a whim, i follow it. if i have an inclination, i investigate it. genuinely i just allow my brain to do the talking and my hands just follow suit.

docs.title: how I tend ideas over time
docs.text: similar in concept to [#how notes grow], i have a random button on my end too! it takes me to a random note and i re-read it and make changes as feel fitting. plus if it's a seedling i go through and do some research to add sources and images.

docs.title: what this garden is not
docs.text: this is not a guaranteed source of factual information. while i do my best to avoid verifiably false information, i also have opinions, speculations, and some times just fuck up. this is also not a space for hatred. politics is one thing, and i absolutely encourage it both in my own investigations into my mind, but also people's responses and critiques of my writing. that being said if your idea of politics is wether or not someone deserves basic human rights (see: food, water, shelter, life, liberty, and the ability to pursue happiness for themselves), then you and i have nothing to talk about. i do not accept arguments in which anyone (and i do mean anyone) is to be treated less for simply existing as they are.

docs.title: an invitation
docs.text:
if you've made it this far, first of all thank you for taking the time to read this! i really do pour my heart into this site, and it means the world to me that my words are reaching other people. that being said, do you disagree with everything i have ever said? maybe reflect on that a little. but do you genuinely have a question, comment, or concern about something i've said? then please reach out! here is a link to my linktree. and i also have giscus discussions embedded on most pages.

For the project overview and local development guide, turn to the Digital Garden README.

docs.title: this is now your lesson plan
break the sub-goals into specific questions (i once again use wikipedia to find these because i still usually have no clue wtf im talking about)
docs.text:
• how to draw
    • materials of the craft
      • what do i need to get started?
      • what do the professionals use?
      • what are the materials specifically used for?
    • anatomy
      • what is the difference between human/animal/plant anatomy?
      • is it best to draw anatomy still or in motion?
    • still life
      • how to draw an apple? (too specific)
      • what is a still life?
      • are still lives the key to unlocking my true potential (probably too vast a question to tackle all at once but you do you)
    • lighting and shading
      • where does light come from and how do i show that?
      • what are the different shading techniques?
      • etc.

docs.title: how to manage too many hobbies at once
docs.text:
1. make a list of everything in progress/ that you want to start now
  2. come up with a reasonable goal or benchmark for each
    1. eg. 1 chapter, 10 minutes, 1 row, etc.
  3. work on each thing in a rotational cycle (this is not a requirement, just what makes it easier for me)
    1. eg. mon i read a chapter out of my 1st book and do a row of knitting and then spend 15 minutes researching something im interested in, wednes i watch an episode of an ongoing tv show read a chapter out of my second book and try a new recipe for dinner, etc.
  4. make a list of all the future things you want to do
  5. give yourself a milestone to achieve before you start
    1. eg. i can start a new fiction book when i finish the last, i can start learning how to knit after i finish this diamond painting, etc.

docs.title: improve your notes to avoid stagnation
docs.text:
this kinda goes hand in hand with one of the core principles of digital gardening, but id argue that it is important for all note taking

  • summarize your own notes
  • redefine key terms
  • draw connections
  • paraphrase
  • ask new questions

in note review there are a few tips - only write the things that matter in the review notes - cut the fluff - big ideas only -summaries, overviews, conclusions - train of thought on how you got to your stance - only if not widely apparent - terms and definitions - examples - only really important in practical studies where you will need to replicate a formula - cooking - physics - math - outline method is the goat for handwriting notes as you don't have space constraints to worry about - esp if you are color coding your headings to your notes on them in recursive reading + 3-pass method - cornell method is how i want to start keeping my notes in obsidian but i don't really know to get started after i have already made a mess of things - maybe use it as my daily note template?

docs.title: leitner my goat
docs.text:
• leitner created a technique involving 5 boxes and flashcards
  • each box is studied at a different interval
    • 1 day
    • 3 days
    • 7 days
    • 14 days
    • 30 days
  • every time u get an answer right it moves up a box
    • every time u get it wrong, go all the way back to the first box

docs.title: recursive reading + 3 pass method
docs.text:
• bring prior knowledge of the subject
  • read once with the intent to garner the most important info
    • headlines
    • summary
    • the first and last sentence of each major body of text
    • diagrams and charts
    • note key terms and vocab
  • ask pertinent questions
  • read again thoroughly
  • ask pertinent questions + define all terms
  • actively recall what you just read in your own words
  • evaluate what you just read
  • apply the reading to other learning and life situations

docs.title: this is all cyclical not linear
spiders are the wisest of us all
docs.text: they cast their silk out from their body, knowing not where it will land, yet once it does, they immediately work to call that place their own. if that place gets torn away from them, they consume whats left of the home they built and use that to make their next home elsewhere. they live by the wind and they offer no complaints to where it takes them. they don't have to know their destination before they begin.

docs.title: stop auditioning for your own life
docs.text: you already know, deep down, what it is that you are meant to do. stop trying to earn the right to be where you are, and instead be present with yourself. you have no worth to earn, you are born with it intrinsic to your being. you have no place of belonging you need to strive for, the people who matter saved your seat already. why are you waiting to be chosen. choose yourself. rejection is not failure.

docs.title: the magic of time blocking
docs.text:
shits great

  • no but seriously breaking your day down into blocks is scientifically one of the best ways to manage your time.
  • if you prioritize heavier loads (mental, physical, emotional, etc.) during times when you are consistently more energized then you will be more productive in the times you aren't due to having easier more manageable tasks
  • block out your energy peaks and hard tasks
    • then make a to-do list of all the easier stuff and do it when time permits (especially when you aren't feeling too hot. accomplishments at hard times can increase motivation and general feelings of wellness)

docs.title: the trad wifeification of self
docs.text: yeah so i, an adult man, feel the draw towards being a house spouse more with every day. it's not out of desire to not work, or even to serve anyone else, but out of a pure desire to take care of my home, my self, and my loved ones. does anyone else feel this way? i imagine as the world grows more hostile, something in my brain chemistry adapted to want my home to be the safest and most comforting it could be. a shelter from the storm if you will. i think having a place like that is a need that not nearly enough people have (as i believe everyone should), and it can affect anyone even the housed.

docs.title: what keeping house is like when you never learned how
docs.text:
i should say clarify that i was taught the basics; how to put laundry into the wash, how to run a dishwasher, how to vacuum. what i didn't learn is how often you should change your linens, is dusting really necessary, and i definitely missed a lesson in how to create a welcoming environment free of mess and decay.

today i will explain how i learned these things on my own in my mid-twenties and why it really is important for everyone to know, not just stay-at-homes.

docs.title: why are you really interested in learning
docs.text:
i have an inate love for learning instilled in me by my family when i was very young.

my abuela was a nurse and still is one of the wisest and most storied individuals i know. my abuelo tinkered with his computer day in and day out, and taught me how to do the same. my titi's are brilliant and amazingly talented women who nurtured my every interest, from art to history to video games and so much more. my aunt is an acupuncturist who taught me to investigate the natural world and the human body. my cousins lent me all of their knowledge of the real world and how to carry myself with pride. my mother is an english major, amazing communicator, and a writer that i sincerely hope will some day publish her works so the world can experience the marvel that is her mind.

i can't not want to learn. it's in my blood.

docs.title: why you need to set end goals on everything even your learning
docs.text: i don't mean to ever stop learning, but since starting my personal curriculum, i have found an increasing need to pace myself. how do i know when i have researched a topic enough for now? how do i know this art piece is finished? how do i stop myself from spiraling and editing the same short essay for weeks on end?
